paper.title: Knowledge Efficient Federated Continual Learning for Industrial Edge Systems
affiliations: Shien-Ming Wu School of Intelligent Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China
School of Mechanical and Automotive Engineering, South China University of Technology, Guangzhou, China
China Academy of Information and Communications Technology, Beijing, China
paper.venue: IEEE Transactions on Network Science and Engineering, vol. 12, no. 3, pp. 2107-2120, May/June 2025 (DOI 10.1109/TNSE.2025.3544614)
paper.one_liner: Federated continual learning that splits models into a meta-learned shared encoder plus task-specific heads stored in a server-side key-value pool retrieved by task embedding.
paper.summary: Industrial edge devices (e.g., vibration sensors on bearings) see data that differs across factories/clients (inter-client heterogeneity) and also drifts over time within each client as operating conditions change (intra-client heterogeneity). FedAvg assumes static client data, and naive training on new conditions causes catastrophic forgetting. MeCo is a federated continual learning method that splits every client model into a task-invariant part u (the early layers, shared and averaged across clients) and a task-specific part v (last residual block plus classifier). The shared part is trained with a MAML-inspired alternating scheme: on each task the client first adapts v on a support split, then updates u on a query split with v fixed, and the server averages u. Every finished task-specific part v is stored on the server in a knowledge pool keyed by a task embedding (mean feature vector of a few samples). When a client starts a new task it sends its embedding, the server returns the top-K most similar stored v's (cosine distance), and the client blends them in with learned attention weights to jump-start learning. On a bearing fault benchmark built from CWRU and SCUT-FD, MeCo reaches 92.26% mean average accuracy (about 2 points above FedWeIT), lower forgetting, and 1.74x lower server-to-client traffic than FedWeIT. There is no unlearning component and no formal theory.
paper.problem: Existing FL methods handle inter-client (spatial) data heterogeneity but assume each client's data is static, which fails in industrial edge systems where sensor data streams drift over time (intra-client, temporal heterogeneity). Retraining from scratch on every drift is too expensive, sequential training causes catastrophic forgetting, replay-based FCL needs memory that edge devices lack and raises privacy/communication concerns, and full-model knowledge transfer (e.g., FedWeIT rehearsing all task parameters) costs communication that grows with the number of tasks.
paper.core_idea: Decompose the model into a shared task-invariant encoder u and small task-specific heads v. Learn u with a meta-learning (support/query, alternating) procedure so it captures features common to all tasks and is robust to forgetting, aggregate it by FedAvg, and keep every task-specific head v on the server in a key-value knowledge pool keyed by a task embedding. New tasks query the pool and fuse only the top-K most similar heads, so knowledge is transferred selectively (reducing interference) and communication scales with K rather than with the total number of tasks.
paper.setting: Federated continual learning (synchronous; one server, N edge clients, each with a private sequential task stream; domain-incremental CL claimed; no replay buffer on clients); application: industrial bearing fault diagnosis from vibration time series converted to CWT images
contributions: MeCo, an FCL method for industrial edge systems combining Meta task-invariant knowledge consolidation and Consistent task-specific knowledge transfer, targeting both inter-client and intra-client data heterogeneity.

A server-side key-value knowledge pool of task-specific parameters, with task-embedding-based top-K selection (cosine distance) and attention-weighted fusion; positioned as orthogonal to rehearsal and suited to resource-constrained edges (no client-side sample storage).
Communication/computation complexity comparison (Table II): MeCo O(NP + NKV) communication vs FedWeIT O(NP + NTV).

Experiments on Overlapped-FD (CWRU + SCUT-FD bearing data, 150 classes, 30 tasks) and CIFAR-100 scalability tests, with ablations on components, backbones (MobileNet, ResNet18/50, ViT-B/16), distance metrics, pool size and K.
method_steps: Setup: model q = u o v. Task-invariant u maps input (CWT time-frequency image of a 1024-step vibration window) to a b-dim feature space; task-specific v (for ResNet: last residual block + classifier) maps features to labels. Server holds global u^(0); each client holds v_i^(0); knowledge pool P is empty; attention weights alpha_i^(0) are initialised (Alg. 1, line 1).
Round t: server broadcasts u^(t-1) to all clients; each client sets u_i^(t) = u^(t) (Alg. 1, lines 3-5).
Client randomly splits its current task data T_i^(t) into a support set T_{i,s} and a query set T_{i,q} (line 6).
Client computes the task embedding k_i^(t) = (1/|T_{i,s}|) * sum_j u_i^(t)(x_j) over support samples (Eq. 7; e.g., 32 samples suffice on CWRU) and uploads this b-dim vector to the server (line 7).

Server computes cosine distance Pi(k_i^(t), k_m) to every key in the pool and selects the K entries with smallest total distance (Eq. 8), then sends their task-specific parameters B_i^(t) = {v_s} to the client (lines 8-9; S2C cost O(NKV)).

Client builds a jump-started head v_i^(t) = alpha_i^(t) (elementwise*) B_i^(t) + v_i^(t-1), i.e., its own previous head plus attention-weighted retrieved heads (Eq. 9, line 10). How alpha is trained is not specified in detail.

ClientUpdate (Alg. 2): inner update - freeze u and take tau_v SGD steps (step gamma_v) on v using the support set; outer update - freeze the updated v^+ and take tau_u SGD steps (step gamma_u) on u using the query set; return (u^+, v^+). In experiments: 5 local epochs per round, Adam lr 1e-3, weight decay 1e-5, batch 64, early stop after 3 epochs without improvement.
Client uploads u_i and v_i to the server (line 12; C2S cost O(NP)).

Server aggregates the shared part by plain averaging u^(t) = (1/N) sum_i u_i (FedAvg on u only, line 13) and stores each (k_i, v_i^(t)) as a new key-value entry in the knowledge pool (line 14); stored entries are deliberately no longer linked to their client or round.
Repeat for subsequent rounds/tasks (60 communication rounds, 6 tasks per client in main experiments); u is refined during meta-training and fixed in meta-testing.

key_definitions.name: Inter-client data heterogeneity
key_definitions.plain: Different clients (machines/factories) have different data distributions at the same time (spatial non-IID); this is what classic FL work targets.
key_definitions.formal: D_i differs from D_j for clients i != j

key_definitions.name: Intra-client data heterogeneity (data drift)
key_definitions.plain: The data distribution of a single client changes over time as new tasks/operating conditions arrive; old task data is no longer available.
key_definitions.formal: client i sees a stream T_i^(1), ..., T_i^(t); T_i^(t) is only available at round t

key_definitions.name: Domain-incremental CL (domain-CL)
key_definitions.plain: Each task keeps the same label set but the input distribution changes; claimed to be the common industrial case and the paper's focus (though the benchmark has 5 distinct classes per task, so the exact label protocol is unclear).

key_definitions.name: Regularized CL objective
key_definitions.plain: Per-task loss plus a penalty for moving away from the previous task's parameters, summed over the task sequence.
key_definitions.formal: f_i(q_i^(t); q_i^(t-1), T_i^(t)) = F_i(q_i^(t); T_i^(t)) + lambda R(q_i^(t), q_i^(t-1)); min sum_t f_i (Eqs. 3-4)

key_definitions.name: FCL objective
key_definitions.plain: Average over clients and over each client's task sequence, where each client may use knowledge from all clients' previous parameters (spatio-temporal knowledge).
key_definitions.formal: min (1/N) sum_{i=1..N} sum_{t=1..N_i} f_i(q_i^(t); q_{1:n}^(t-1), T_i^(t)) (Eq. 5); with decomposition q = u o v (Eq. 6)

key_definitions.name: Parameter decomposition
key_definitions.plain: Split the network into task-invariant parameters u (shared feature extractor) and task-specific parameters v (small head per task).
key_definitions.formal: u: R^d -> R^b, v: R^b -> Y, q_i^(t) = u_i^(t) o v_i^(t)

key_definitions.name: Knowledge pool
key_definitions.plain: Server-side store of all historical task-specific parameter sets from all clients, each keyed by a task embedding; entries are detached from client identity.
key_definitions.formal: B = {(k_1, v_1), ..., (k_M, v_M)}, k_m in R^b; key set K = {k_m}

key_definitions.name: Task embedding
key_definitions.plain: A fixed-length summary of a task: the average feature vector produced by the shared encoder on a small support subset.
key_definitions.formal: k_i^(t) = (1/|T_{i,s}|) sum_j u_i^(t)(x_j) (Eq. 7; written with (u(x_j), y_j) pairs in the paper)

key_definitions.name: Consistent parameter selection (top-K)
key_definitions.plain: Server picks the K pool entries whose keys are closest (cosine distance) to the new task's embedding.
key_definitions.formal: K_i^(t) = argmin over {s_1..s_K} subset of [1,M] of sum_{k=1..K} Pi(k_i^(t), k_{s_k}) (Eq. 8)

key_definitions.name: Attention-weighted fusion
key_definitions.plain: The new head equals the client's previous head plus an elementwise-attention-weighted combination of the retrieved heads.

key_definitions.name: Jump-starting
key_definitions.plain: Borrowed from RL: learning a good prior/initialisation for the current task by combining knowledge from previous tasks with a little new data.

key_definitions.name: Mean (macro-averaged) Average Accuracy, MAA
key_definitions.plain: For each client, average test accuracy over all tasks seen so far; then average over clients.

key_definitions.name: Forgetting
key_definitions.plain: How much a task's accuracy has dropped from right after it was learned to now, averaged over all earlier tasks.

key_definitions.name: S2C / C2S communication
key_definitions.plain: Total bytes sent server-to-client and client-to-server during training (reported in GB).

theory.name: No theorems/lemmas
theory.statement_plain: The paper contains no formal theorems, convergence proofs, or forgetting bounds; its analysis is a problem formulation (Eqs. 1-6) and an asymptotic cost comparison.
theory.significance: Any guarantee (convergence of the alternating u/v updates, forgetting bounds, privacy of embeddings) is an open gap.

theory.name: Communication/computation complexity (Sec. IV-D, Table II)
theory.statement_plain: Per round, MeCo communicates O(NP + NKV) (FedAvg-style u exchange plus top-K task-specific heads) and costs O(E n_c P + K V^2) computation per client; FedWeIT needs O(NP + NTV) communication and O(E n_c P + P + P^2) computation; FedAvg+EWC O(NP) / O(E n_c P + P^2); FedAvg+MAS O(NP) / O(E n_c P + P); FedAvg+iCaRL O(NP) / O(E n_c P + n_c^2 P); FedAvg O(NP) / O(E n_c P).
theory.assumptions: N clients, P model params, E local epochs, n_c samples per client, T tasks, V size of one task-specific head, K retrieved heads; derivation is informal (the K V^2 term for selection is not justified).
theory.significance: Explains the S2C saving vs FedWeIT: MeCo transfers K heads instead of heads from all T tasks, so cost does not grow with the task history.

theory.name: Task-distribution coverage assumption (Sec. IV-B)
theory.statement_plain: The data distribution of a new task is assumed to lie within the aggregate distribution of all historical tasks, so relevant knowledge can be found in the pool.
theory.assumptions: Stated as a 'mild assumption'; not formalised or tested.
theory.significance: Justifies similarity-based retrieval; it fails for genuinely novel tasks (cold start), where the retrieved heads may inject irrelevant knowledge.

paper.complexity: Learning: communication O(NP + NKV) per round (S2C: top-K heads O(NKV) plus global u; C2S: u and v), computation O(E n_c P + K V^2) per client per round. Empirically on Overlapped-FD/ResNet18: S2C 3.1 GB vs FedWeIT 5.4 GB (5.4/3.1 = 1.74x, the headline claim) and vs FedAvg 2.6 GB; C2S 2.6 GB for all FL methods. Server storage grows linearly with the number of (client, task) entries M times head size V; no client-side replay storage (vs iCaRL buffer of 12,000 samples). Training time per batch of 16 across 5 clients with ResNet18: MeCo 142 ms vs FedWeIT 150 ms vs FedAvg 125 ms; inference 87 / 100 / 75 ms. Unlearning cost: not discussed (the paper has no deletion mechanism).

datasets: Overlapped-FD (constructed): CWRU + SCUT-FD bearing fault data; CWRU split by 4 motor speeds (1730/1750/1772/1797 rpm) plus 6 pairwise speed combinations = 10 conditions x 10 classes x 2 tasks = 100 classes/20 tasks; SCUT-FD split by 500/800/1100/1400 rpm plus combinations = 10 conditions x 5 classes x 1 task = 50 classes/10 tasks; total 150 classes, 5 classes per task, tasks randomly assigned to clients; no task-boundary information used
CWRU bearing dataset (Case Western Reserve University; drive-end/fan-end deep groove ball bearings, fault types IF, OF, RoF plus normal, loads 0-3)
SCUT-FD (real industrial bearing fault dataset from SCUT, ref [36])
models: ResNet18 (main, trained from scratch, ~11.7M params; last residual block + classifier = task-specific)
Input: vibration time series converted to time-frequency images by continuous wavelet transform over 1024-step windows (0-12 kHz); no recurrent/temporal sequence model is used
baselines: STL (single-task learning, separate model per task)
Not included: FedProx, FedKNOW, FedPer (FedPer only discussed in Remark 1); FedAvg+MAS appears only in the complexity table
metrics: MAA (called Mean Average Accuracy in abstract, Macro-averaged Accuracy in Sec. V)
headline_results: Overlapped-FD, ResNet18, 5 clients x 6 tasks, 60 rounds (Table IV): MeCo MAA 92.26 (+/-0.17), F1 91.25 (+/-0.34), forgetting 0.02, S2C 3.1 GB, C2S 2.6 GB
FedWeIT 90.13 / 87.45 / 0.03 / 5.4 GB / 2.6 GB -> MeCo +2.13 MAA and 1.74x cheaper S2C (5.4/3.1)
Local-only: STL 82.36, EWC 80.82, MAS 80.63, iCaRL 82.42, OML 82.57 MAA; all FL methods beat local CL
Ablation (Table V): w/o consistent knowledge transfer MAA 81.66, F1 79.2; w/o meta consolidation MAA 85.74, F1 84.4 (paper's printed deltas -10.50/-11.05/-6.42/-6.85 do not all match the arithmetic)
Backbones (Table VI) MAA MeCo vs FedWeIT vs FedAvg: MobileNet 88.92/86.71/84.55; ResNet50 94.03/91.99/88.72; ViT-B/16 95.41/92.61/89.52
Distance metric (Table VII): cosine 92.26 > KL 91.77 > Euclidean 91.13 MAA
Fig. 9 (read from plot, approximate): MAA rises from ~83% to ~92% as pool size grows 5 to 25; best K is about 3 (~92.3%), K=1 ~87.5%, slight drop for K=4-5 (irrelevant knowledge)
Scalability (Table VIII): CIFAR-100 N=5 to 10 (N_i=10): MeCo 70.01 to 69.95 MAA, forgetting 2.75 to 3.40%; FedAvg 66.31 to 60.14; FedAvg+iCaRL 67.98 to 63.19
Overlapped-FD N_i=6 to 12: MeCo 92.26 to 91.72 MAA, forgetting 2.20 to 2.93%; FedAvg 88.46 to 85.06 (forgetting 12.60 to 14.70%)

limitations: No theoretical guarantees (no convergence or forgetting bounds); the task-coverage assumption is informal and untested on novel tasks.
Evaluation is mostly one constructed fault-diagnosis benchmark with 5-10 simulated clients and 3 runs; CIFAR-100 only for scalability.
Task boundaries are effectively known/discrete; authors note task-transition detection would be needed in real deployments.
The server keeps every client's task-specific parameters and receives task embeddings; privacy of these artefacts is claimed but not analysed (no DP, no attack evaluation).
Knowledge pool grows without bound (one entry per client per task); pool storage and retrieval cost at scale are not studied (Fig. 9 only up to 30 entries).

Pool entries are deliberately decoupled from their client/round, and retrieved heads are additively merged into other clients' heads, so a client's knowledge spreads with no record - a problem for deletion requests.

Training of attention weights alpha and the exact meta-learning objective are under-specified; the 'meta' step is a first-order alternating support/query scheme rather than true MAML bi-level optimisation.

Inconsistencies: Sec. III-B says pre-trained models are used but Sec. V-A says no pre-trained weights; forgetting is reported as 0.10 (FedAvg) in Table IV but 12.60% for the apparently same setting in Table VIII; '1997 rpm' vs 1797 in Table III; 'C_4^2 = 10' (actually 4 + 6 conditions); domain-CL is claimed but tasks have distinct classes; ablation deltas do not match.
Weak baseline coverage: no FedProx, FedKNOW, or other parameter-decomposition FCL methods; FedPer only discussed.
future_work: Apply MeCo beyond industrial fault diagnosis to other domains and tasks.
Extend the framework to continual pre-training tasks.
Add task-transition detection for non-discrete, realistic task boundaries.
Balance the growing communication/computation overhead as the number of clients increases.
paper.relevance_to_efficient_unlearning: MeCo has no unlearning, but its structure shows where an unlearning mechanism would have to go in federated continual learning. Forgetting a client or a task would need three things: (1) deleting that client's/task's (key, head) entries from the server knowledge pool, which is cheap only if provenance is kept, while MeCo deliberately drops the client/round link; (2) undoing the spread of those heads into other clients' heads through Eq. 9 (v_i^(t) = alpha * B + v_i^(t-1)) and on into later pool entries, which needs a retrieval/lineage log (the additive form even suggests an approximate 'subtract alpha*v_s' correction, but later gradient steps make it inexact); (3) removing the client's influence from the FedAvg-aggregated, meta-learned task-invariant encoder u, which is a standard federated-unlearning problem (retrain from a checkpoint, or shard clients SISA-style). The parameter decomposition itself is a useful efficiency idea: if retrieval were turned off or tracked, task knowledge sits in small isolated modules whose deletion is exact and costs O(V), much like SISA's isolation or adapter-based CL+unlearning (BID-LoRA). Task-embedding keys could also find the pool entries relevant to a forget request. Pitfalls to avoid: shared-encoder entanglement, cross-client mixing of heads, and an unbounded pool that keeps everything forever.
open_questions: Design a provenance-tracked knowledge pool (record client, task, and which entries each head retrieved via Eq. 9) and an exact client/task deletion procedure; measure its cost against retraining MeCo from scratch.
How should the shared, FedAvg-aggregated encoder u be unlearned? Compare freezing u after meta-training, checkpoint rollback, and SISA-style client sharding of u, in accuracy vs unlearning time.

Exploit the additive fusion v = alpha*B + v_prev for approximate unlearning (subtract the forgotten head's weighted contribution, then briefly fine-tune), and bound the leftover influence after later local updates.
Task-level continual unlearning in MeCo: does deleting a pool entry actually remove the capability (forget accuracy, membership-inference success), given leakage into u and into other clients' heads?
Privacy audit: can stored heads v or class-conditioned task embeddings k leak client data (membership/attribute inference), and can DP noise on k/v keep retrieval accuracy?
Provide convergence and forgetting guarantees for the alternating u/v (support/query) update under the task-coverage assumption, and handle novel tasks that violate it.

nodes.label: Federated Learning
nodes.description: Distributed training where many clients train a shared model on their local data and send only model updates to a server, so raw data never leaves the client.

nodes.label: Continual Learning
nodes.description: Learning from a sequence of tasks or a non-stationary data stream while keeping performance on earlier tasks, usually without full access to past data.

nodes.label: Federated Continual Learning
nodes.description: Federated learning where each client receives a private sequence of tasks over time, so the system must handle both cross-client heterogeneity and catastrophic forgetting.

nodes.label: Meta-Learning
nodes.description: Learning to learn: optimising a model (often its initialisation or representation) across many tasks so it adapts quickly to new tasks from few examples.

nodes.label: Edge Computing
nodes.description: Running computation and learning close to where data is generated (devices, gateways) instead of only in the cloud, under tight compute, memory and bandwidth limits.

nodes.label: Industrial Edge Systems / IIoT
nodes.description: Industrial Internet of Things deployments where sensors and machines produce continuous time-series streams that are processed on resource-limited edge devices together with a cloud server.

nodes.label: Industrial Fault Diagnosis
nodes.description: Detecting and classifying faults in machinery (e.g., bearing inner/outer race or rolling element faults) from sensor signals such as vibration.

nodes.label: Domain-Incremental Learning
nodes.description: Continual-learning scenario in which the label space stays the same across tasks but the input distribution (domain) changes from task to task.

nodes.label: Data Privacy
nodes.description: Protecting individuals' or organisations' data from exposure or misuse during collection, training and model release.

nodes.label: Personalization
nodes.description: Adapting models to individual clients or users, for example by keeping some client-specific parameters, instead of using only one global model.

nodes.label: Machine Unlearning
nodes.description: Removing the influence of specific training data (samples, clients or tasks) from a trained model without, or more cheaply than, retraining from scratch.

nodes.label: Federated Unlearning
nodes.description: Machine unlearning in federated learning: removing a client's or some samples' contribution from the global model, which is hard because updates are aggregated across many rounds.

nodes.label: Continual Unlearning
nodes.description: Handling interleaved learning and deletion requests over a task stream, e.g., forgetting a specific past task while retaining the others.

nodes.label: Forward Transfer
nodes.description: Positive influence of knowledge from earlier tasks on learning a new task, making it faster or more accurate.

nodes.label: Jump-Starting
nodes.description: Concept from reinforcement-learning transfer: using knowledge from previous tasks plus a little new data to give a new task a good starting point or prior.

nodes.label: Catastrophic Forgetting
nodes.description: When a neural network trained on new data overwrites weights important for earlier tasks, its performance on those tasks drops sharply.

nodes.label: Data Heterogeneity (non-IID)
nodes.description: Clients' local data distributions differ from each other, which slows or biases federated training of a single global model.

nodes.label: Data Drift / Intra-client Heterogeneity
nodes.description: The data distribution seen by a single learner changes over time (e.g., new operating conditions), so data at different times is non-identically distributed.

nodes.label: Communication Cost
nodes.description: The bandwidth and latency of exchanging models, gradients or other data between clients and server, often the bottleneck in federated systems.

nodes.label: Stability-Plasticity Trade-off
nodes.description: The tension between keeping previously learned knowledge stable and staying flexible enough to learn new tasks.

nodes.label: Edge Memory Constraint
nodes.description: Edge devices have limited storage and compute, so methods that keep growing replay buffers or full histories of models may not fit on them.

nodes.label: Inter-client Knowledge Interference
nodes.description: Negative transfer when knowledge from unrelated clients or tasks is merged into a model and hurts its performance on the current task.

nodes.label: Privacy Leakage
nodes.description: Unintended exposure of information about training data through stored samples, transmitted updates or model outputs.

nodes.label: MeCo
nodes.description: Federated continual learning framework that combines a meta-learned shared encoder with a server-side key-value pool of task-specific heads, retrieved by task-embedding similarity.

nodes.label: Meta Task-Invariant Knowledge Consolidation
nodes.description: Training the shared feature extractor with a meta-learning style support/query procedure so it captures features common to all tasks and resists forgetting.

nodes.label: Consistent Task-Specific Knowledge Transfer
nodes.description: Transferring stored task-specific parameters from similar earlier tasks (found by embedding similarity) to initialise or augment the parameters for a new task.

nodes.label: Knowledge Pool
nodes.description: A memory of reusable knowledge items (e.g., parameter modules or prompts) stored as key-value pairs, from which relevant entries are retrieved by matching a query key.

nodes.label: Task Embedding
nodes.description: A fixed-length vector that summarises a task or dataset, often the mean feature of a few samples under a shared encoder, used to compare tasks.

nodes.label: Top-K Similarity Retrieval
nodes.description: Choosing the K stored items whose keys are most similar (smallest distance) to a query vector.

nodes.label: Attention-Weighted Parameter Fusion
nodes.description: Combining several parameter sets into one by adding learned (element-wise) attention-weighted contributions, here on top of a base parameter set.

nodes.label: Alternating Inner/Outer (Support/Query) Update
nodes.description: Optimisation scheme that alternately updates task-specific parameters on a support split with the shared part frozen, then updates the shared part on a query split with the task-specific part frozen.

nodes.label: Parameter Decomposition
nodes.description: Splitting model parameters into a shared/global part and task- or client-specific parts so knowledge can be shared, isolated and transmitted separately.

nodes.label: MAML
nodes.description: Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning: learns an initialisation from which a few gradient steps on a new task's support set give good performance on its query set.

nodes.label: FedAvg
nodes.description: Federated Averaging: clients run local SGD and the server averages their model weights, weighted by data size, each round.

nodes.label: FedWeIT
nodes.description: Federated Weighted Inter-client Transfer: FCL method that splits weights into global and sparse task-adaptive parts and transfers other clients' task-adaptive parameters with attention masks.

nodes.label: EWC
nodes.description: Elastic Weight Consolidation: regularises parameters toward old values, weighted by Fisher-information importance, to reduce forgetting.

nodes.label: MAS
nodes.description: Memory Aware Synapses: regularization-based CL that estimates each parameter's importance from the sensitivity of the network output to it.

nodes.label: iCaRL
nodes.description: Incremental Classifier and Representation Learning: class-incremental method that keeps an exemplar buffer per class and uses nearest-mean-of-exemplars classification.

nodes.label: Experience Replay / Rehearsal
nodes.description: Continual-learning technique that stores (or generates) samples from earlier tasks and mixes them into training on new tasks.

nodes.label: OML
nodes.description: Online-aware Meta-Learning: meta-learns a representation network so that online updates of a small prediction head cause little interference and forgetting.

nodes.label: Single Task Learning (STL)
nodes.description: Baseline that trains a separate model for each task with no knowledge transfer or retention across tasks.

nodes.label: FedPer
nodes.description: Federated learning with personalization layers: base layers are shared and aggregated while top layers stay local to each client.

nodes.label: Regularization-based Continual Learning
nodes.description: Family of CL methods that add a penalty to the loss to keep parameters important for old tasks close to their previous values.

nodes.label: Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT)
nodes.description: Signal transform that turns a 1-D time series into a 2-D time-frequency representation using scaled and shifted wavelets.

nodes.label: Cosine Distance
nodes.description: Dissimilarity between two vectors computed as one minus the cosine of the angle between them; ignores vector magnitude.

nodes.label: Retrain from Scratch
nodes.description: Retraining a model from initialisation on the updated dataset; the simplest exact way to adapt to new data or remove data, but expensive.

nodes.label: CWRU Bearing Dataset
nodes.description: Case Western Reserve University benchmark of accelerometer vibration signals from ball bearings with seeded inner-race, outer-race and ball faults under several motor loads/speeds.
aliases: Case Western Reserve University bearing data

nodes.label: SCUT-FD
nodes.description: Bearing fault diagnosis dataset collected in real industrial scenarios at South China University of Technology, with several rotating speeds.

nodes.label: Overlapped-FD
nodes.description: Federated continual fault-diagnosis benchmark built by splitting CWRU and SCUT-FD by rotating speed (and speed pairs) into 30 five-class tasks assigned to clients.

nodes.label: CIFAR-100
nodes.description: Image classification dataset of 60,000 32x32 colour images in 100 classes.

nodes.label: ResNet-18
nodes.description: 18-layer residual convolutional network with skip connections (about 11.7M parameters).

nodes.label: ResNet-50
nodes.description: 50-layer residual convolutional network with bottleneck blocks (about 25M parameters).

nodes.label: Vision Transformer (ViT)
nodes.description: Transformer applied to sequences of image patches; ViT-B/16 uses 16x16 patches and about 86M parameters.

nodes.label: MobileNetV2
nodes.description: Lightweight CNN for mobile/edge devices built from inverted residual blocks with linear bottlenecks (a few million parameters).

nodes.label: Mean Average Accuracy (MAA)
nodes.description: Continual-learning metric: average test accuracy over all tasks seen so far, here further averaged over clients.

nodes.label: Macro F1
nodes.description: Unweighted mean of F1 scores (over classes or, here, clients), balancing precision and recall.

nodes.label: Forgetting Measure
nodes.description: Average drop from each task's best (just-learned) accuracy to its accuracy after later tasks have been learned.

nodes.label: Communication Overhead
nodes.description: Measured amount of data exchanged between server and clients (e.g., GB server-to-client and client-to-server).

nodes.label: Communication/Computation Complexity Analysis
nodes.description: Asymptotic accounting of per-round bytes exchanged and per-client compute of a federated algorithm as functions of clients, parameters, data and tasks.

nodes.label: Task-Distribution Coverage Assumption
nodes.description: Assumption that a new task's data distribution is contained in the union/aggregate of previously seen task distributions, so relevant past knowledge exists.

edges.note: The paper's main contribution is the MeCo FCL framework for industrial edge systems.
edges.evidence: Contributions: 'We propose MeCo, a novel FCL approach designed for IES.'

cross_paper.note: MeCo isolates task knowledge in per-(client, task) heads stored as separate pool entries, which resembles SISA's isolation; with provenance and retrieval tracking, deleting a client/task could become a constituent-level removal. MeCo has no deletion mechanism and its Eq. 9 cross-client mixing breaks isolation.

Both index task-specific knowledge with task embeddings in continual learning; UnCLe adds task unlearning, which MeCo's knowledge pool lacks, so it suggests how pool entries could support task-level forgetting.

BID-LoRA keeps per-task knowledge in parameter-efficient adapters for joint continual learning and unlearning; MeCo's small task-specific heads play a similar modular role but have no unlearning path.

MeCo's FedAvg-aggregated, meta-learned shared encoder u entangles every client's contribution; honouring a client-deletion request would need a federated-unlearning scheme like FedShard's sharded, efficiency-aware approach.

Ginart et al.'s deletion-efficiency principles (modularity, few dependencies per deletion) give a design target for an unlearnable MeCo knowledge pool, where currently one head can propagate into many others.
